questions.question: Let \(P \neq 0\) be a \(3 \times 3\) real matrix. There exist linearly independent vectors \(x\) and \(y\) such that \(Px = 0\) and \(Py = 0\). The dimension of the range space of \(P\) is
questions.explanation: Given that \(P \neq 0\) is a \(3 \times 3\) real matrix. We are given that there exist two linearly independent vectors \(x\) and \(y\) such that: \[Px = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad Py = 0\] This means that both vectors \(x\) and \(y\) belong to the null space (kernel) of the matrix \(P\). Since \(x\) and \(y\) are linearly independent, the dimension of the null space, also known as the nullity of \(P\), must be at least \(2\): \[\text{Nullity}(P) \ge 2\] According to the Rank-Nullity Theorem, for any \(n \times n\) square matrix: \[\text{Rank}(P) + \text{Nullity}(P) = n\] Here, the matrix \(P\) is of order \(3 \times 3\), so \(n = 3\): \[\text{Rank}(P) = 3 - \text{Nullity}(P)\] Since \(\text{Nullity}(P) \ge 2\): \[\text{Rank}(P) \le 3 - 2 \implies \text{Rank}(P) \le 1\] We are also given that \(P \neq 0\) (it is a non-zero matrix), which implies that its rank must be at least \(1\): \[\text{Rank}(P) \ge 1\] Combining the inequalities \(\text{Rank}(P) \le 1\) and \(\text{Rank}(P) \ge 1\), we get: \[\text{Rank}(P) = 1\] Since the range space of a matrix is its column space, the dimension of the range space is exactly equal to the rank of the matrix: \[\text{Dimension of range space of } P = \text{Rank}(P) = 1\] \[\boxed{\text{(B) 1}}\]

questions.question: The eigenvalues of a \((2 \times 2)\) matrix \(X\) are \(-2\) and \(-3\). The eigenvalues of the matrix \((X + I)^{-1}(X + 5I)\) are
questions.explanation:
If the eigenvalues of \(X\) are \(-2, -3\) and the eigenvalues of the identity matrix \(I\) are \(1, 1\), then the eigenvalues of the matrix shift \((X + I)\) are calculated by adding the corresponding scalar coefficients: \[-2 + 1, \quad -3 + 1 \implies -1, \quad -2\] Consider the given rational matrix polynomial: \[(X + I)^{-1}(X + 5I)\] We can algebraically manipulate the expression to simplify it: \[(X + I)^{-1}(X + 5I) = (X + I)^{-1}(X + I + 4I)\] \[\implies (X + I)^{-1}(X + 5I) = (X + I)^{-1}(X + I) + 4(X + I)^{-1}\] \[\implies (X + I)^{-1}(X + 5I) = I + 4(X + I)^{-1}\] If \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of the base matrix \(X\), then the eigenvalue mapping function for the expression \(I + 4(X + I)^{-1}\) is given by: \[f(\lambda) = 1 + 4(\lambda + 1)^{-1}\] Now, we evaluate this mapping function for each specific eigenvalue of \(X\):
  • For \(\lambda = -2\):
    \[f(-2) = 1 + 4(-2 + 1)^{-1} = 1 + 4(-1)^{-1} = 1 - 4 = -3\]
  • For \(\lambda = -3\):
    \[f(-3) = 1 + 4(-3 + 1)^{-1} = 1 + 4(-2)^{-1} = 1 - 2 = -1\]
\[\therefore \text{The eigenvalues of } I + 4(X + I)^{-1} \text{ are } -3, -1.\] Hence, the correct option is (c). \[\boxed{\text{(C) $-1, -3$}}\]
Key points
  • Spectral Mapping Theorem: If \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of \(A\), then for any rational function \(r(x)\), \(r(\lambda)\) is an eigenvalue of \(r(A)\), provided the function is well-defined.
  • Inverse Eigenvalue Rule: If a matrix \(M\) has non-zero eigenvalues \(\mu_i\), then its inverse matrix \(M^{-1}\) has the corresponding eigenvalues \(\dfrac{1}{\mu_i}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Direct Scalar Multiplication Mistakes: Avoid applying properties blindly without decomposing the matrix expression first; trying to calculate \((X+I)^{-1}\) and \((X+5I)\) eigenvalues separately and multiplying them directly can cause confusion if order isn't preserved.
  • Division by Zero Check: Always verify that the eigenvalues of the shifted matrix \((X + I)\) are non-zero (here they are \(-1\) and \(-2\)) before assuming that the inverse operation \((X+I)^{-1}\) is valid.

questions.question: The matrix \[P = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\] rotates a vector about the axis \[\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\] by an angle of
questions.explanation:
Given the rotation matrix: \[P = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\] The trace of a \(3 \times 3\) proper rotation matrix \(R\) that rotates a vector about a given axis by an angle \(\theta\) satisfies the geometric formula: \[\text{Tr}(R) = 1 + 2\cos\theta\] First, let us calculate the trace of the given matrix \(P\) by summing its principal diagonal entries: \[\text{Tr}(P) = 0 + 0 + 0 = 0\] Now, equate the trace value to the rotation equation formula: \[1 + 2\cos\theta = 0\] \[\implies 2\cos\theta = -1\] \[\implies \cos\theta = -\dfrac{1}{2}\] Solving for \(\theta\) within the standard geometric range \([0^\circ, 180^\circ]\): \[\theta = \cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 120^\circ\] \[\boxed{\text{(D) $120^\circ$}}\]
Key points
  • Axis of Rotation Verification: The axis of rotation corresponds to the invariant eigenvector under the transformation matrix. Indeed, \[P\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\], confirming it has an eigenvalue of \(\lambda = 1\).
  • Trace-Angle Relation: For any standard \(3 \times 3\) proper orthogonal rotation matrix, its trace represents the sum of its eigenvalues (\(1 + e^{i\theta} + e^{-i\theta} = 1 + 2\cos\theta\)).

questions.question: If \(z = x + jy\), where \(x\) and \(y\) are real, the value of \(\left|e^{j\,z}\right|\) is
questions.explanation:
Given the complex variable \(z = x + jy\), to find the magnitude of \(e^{jz}\). Substitute \(z\) into the exponent: \[jz = j(x + jy) = jx + j^2y\] Since \(j^2 = -1\): \[jz = -y + jx\] Hence, \[e^{jz} = e^{-y + jx} = e^{-y} \cdot e^{jx}\] Since, \[|e^{jz}| = |e^{-y}| \cdot |e^{jx}|\] Since \(x\) and \(y\) are real numbers, \(e^{-y}\) is a positive real quantity, so \(|e^{-y}| = e^{-y}\). By Euler's formula, \(|e^{jx}| = |\cos(x) + j\sin(x)| = \sqrt{\cos^2(x) + \sin^2(x)} = 1\). Therefore:\[|e^{jz}| = e^{-y} \cdot 1 = e^{-y}\] \[\boxed{D. \ e^{-y}}\]
Key points
  • Magnitude of Complex Exponentials: For any real value \(\theta\), \(|e^{j\theta}| = 1\).
  • The magnitude of \(e^{z}\) depends entirely on its real part: \(|e^{u + jv}| = e^u\).

questions.question: The value of \(\oint \dfrac{\sin z}{z} \, dz\), where the contour of integration is a simple closed curve around the origin, is
questions.explanation:
To evaluate the contour integral: \[I = \oint \frac{\sin z}{z} \, dz\] around a simple closed curve enclosing the origin. Analyzing the singularity at \(z = 0\) with the Taylor series expansion of \(\sin z\): \[\sin z = z - \frac{z^3}{3!} + \frac{z^5}{5!} - \cdots\] Dividing by \(z\): \[\frac{\sin z}{z} = 1 - \frac{z^2}{3!} + \frac{z^4}{5!} - \cdots\] Because this expansion contains only non-negative powers of \(z\), the point \(z = 0\) is a removable singularity. The function \(f(z) = \frac{\sin z}{z}\) can be redefined at \(z = 0\) to be \(1\), making it analytic everywhere inside and on the closed curve. By Cauchy’s Integral Theorem, if a function is analytic everywhere inside and on a simple closed path, its loop integral is zero: \[I = 0\] \[\boxed{A. 0}\]
Key points
  • Removable Singularity: If \(\lim_{z \to a} f(z)\) exists and is finite, then \(z = a\) is a removable singularity, and the residue at that point is \(0\).

questions.question: One of the roots of the equation \(x^3 = j\), where \(j\) is the positive square root of \(-1\), is
questions.explanation: Given the algebraic equation: \[x^3 = j\] where \(j = \sqrt{-1}\). We need to find one of its roots. We know, \[j = 0 + 1j = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) + j\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = e^{j\pi/2}\] To find all unique cube roots,by the periodicity of \(2k\pi\): \[x^3 = e^{j\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + 2k\pi\right)} \quad \text{for } k = 0, 1, 2\] Taking the cube root of both sides: \[x = e^{j\left(\frac{\pi}{6} + \frac{2k\pi}{3}\right)}\] Finding the root corresponding to \(k = 0\): \[x_0 = e^{j\pi/6} = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) + j\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\] \[\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \quad \text{and} \quad \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\] We get,\[x_0 = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + j\frac{1}{2}\] \[\boxed{B. \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + j\frac{1}{2}}\]

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: For input \(x(t)\), an ideal impulse sampling system produces the output \[y(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x(kT)\,\delta(t-kT)\] where \(\delta(t)\) is the Dirac delta function. The system is
questions.explanation:
Given, \[y(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x(kT)\,\delta(t-kT)\] (i) Linearity:
For input \(x_1(t)\), output will be \(y_1(t)\). \[y_1(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x_1(kT)\,\delta(t-kT)\] Multiplying both sides by scalar quantity \(a\), \[a\,y_1(t) = a\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x_1(kT)\,\delta(t-kT) \tag{i}\] For input \(x_2(t)\), output will be \(y_2(t)\). \[y_2(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x_2(kT)\,\delta(t-kT)\] Multiplying both sides by scalar quantity \(b\), \[b\,y_2(t) = b\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x_2(kT)\,\delta(t-kT) \tag{ii}\] Adding equations (i) and (ii), \[a\,y_1(t)+b\,y_2(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} \left[ a\,x_1(kT)+b\,x_2(kT) \right] \delta(t-kT) \tag{iii}\] Now, let the system have input \[a\,x_1(t)+b\,x_2(t)\] and corresponding output be \(y_3(t)\). \[y_3(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} \left[ a\,x_1(kT)+b\,x_2(kT) \right] \delta(t-kT) \tag{iv}\] From equations (iii) and (iv), \[y_3(t)=a\,y_1(t)+b\,y_2(t)\] Therefore, the system follows the principle of superposition. Hence, the system is linear. (ii) Time Variance:
In a time invariant system, any delay provided in input must be reflected in output. Let the input be delayed by \(t_0\), then corresponding output is \(y_1(t)\). \[y_1(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x(kT-t_0)\,\delta(t-kT) \tag{v}\] Now, output \(y(t)\) is delayed by \(t_0\), \[y(t-t_0) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x(kT)\,\delta(t-t_0-kT) \tag{vi}\] From equations (v) and (vi), \[y_1(t)\neq y(t-t_0)\] Thus, the system is time varying. (D) linear and time-varying

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: A linear time-invariant causal system has frequency response given in polar form as\[H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\omega^{2}}}\angle\left(-\tan^{-1}\omega\right).\]For the input\[x(t)=\sin t,\]the output is
questions.explanation:
Theory: For an LTI system, a sinusoidal input undergoes only amplitude scaling and phase shifting. Given,\[H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\omega^{2}}} \angle\left(-\tan^{-1}\omega\right),\]and\[x(t)=\sin t.\]The input frequency is\[\omega=1~\text{rad/s}.\]Hence,\[|H(j1)| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+1^2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2},\]and\[\angle H(j1) = -\tan^{-1}(1) = -\frac{\pi}{4}.\]Therefore,\[y(t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt2} \sin\left(t-\frac{\pi}{4}\right).\] \[\boxed{\text{(D) }\displaystyle \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\sin\left(t-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}\]
Key points
  • A sinusoidal input remains sinusoidal after passing through an LTI system.
  • Output amplitude is multiplied by \(|H(j\omega)|\).
  • Output phase is shifted by \(\angle H(j\omega)\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not change the input frequency.
  • Evaluate the frequency response at the input frequency only.
  • Apply both magnitude scaling and phase shift.

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: An analog signal is sampled at \(9~\text{kHz}\). The sequence so obtained is filtered by an FIR filter with transfer function\[H(z)=1-z^{-6}.\]One of the analog frequencies for which the magnitude response of the filter is zero is
questions.explanation:
Theory: The frequency response is obtained by substituting \(z=e^{j\omega}\). Given,\[H(z)=1-z^{-6}.\]Therefore,\[H(e^{j\omega}) = 1-e^{-j6\omega}.\]Its magnitude is\[|H(e^{j\omega})| = \sqrt{(1-\cos6\omega)^2+\sin^26\omega}.\]Using\[(1-\cos6\omega)^2+\sin^26\omega = 2-2\cos6\omega = 4\sin^23\omega,\]we obtain\[|H(e^{j\omega})| = 2|\sin3\omega|.\]For the magnitude response to be zero,\[\sin3\omega=0,\]which gives\[3\omega=n\pi.\]The digital and analog frequencies are related by\[\omega=\frac{2\pi f}{f_s}.\]Substituting \(f_s=9~\text{kHz}\),\[3\left(\frac{2\pi f}{9000}\right)=n\pi,\]which gives\[f=\frac{n\times9000}{6}.\]For \(n=1\),\[f=1500~\text{Hz}=1.5~\text{kHz}.\]Hence,\[\boxed{\text{(C) }1.5~\text{kHz}}\]
Key points
  • Evaluate the frequency response using \(z=e^{j\omega}\).
  • Use the identity \(2-2\cos\theta=4\sin^2(\theta/2)\).
  • Relate digital and analog frequencies using \(\omega=\dfrac{2\pi f}{f_s}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not forget to take the magnitude before equating it to zero.
  • Use the sampling frequency while converting from \(\omega\) to \(f\).
  • Remember that the smallest positive solution corresponds to \(n=1\).

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: The transfer function \(H(z)\) of a fourth-order linear phase FIR system is given by\[H(z)=\left(1+2z^{-1}+3z^{-2}\right)G(z).\]Then \(G(z)\) is
questions.explanation:
Theory: A linear-phase FIR filter has a symmetric impulse response,\[h[n]=h[M-1-n],\]where \(M\) is the number of filter coefficients. Let\[G(z)=A_0+A_1z^{-1}+A_2z^{-2}.\]Then,\[H(z) = (1+2z^{-1}+3z^{-2}) (A_0+A_1z^{-1}+A_2z^{-2}).\]Expanding,\[H(z) = A_0 +(2A_0+A_1)z^{-1} +(3A_0+2A_1+A_2)z^{-2} +(3A_1+2A_2)z^{-3} +3A_2z^{-4}.\]Hence,\[\begin{aligned} h[0]&=A_0,\\ h[1]&=2A_0+A_1,\\ h[2]&=3A_0+2A_1+A_2,\\ h[3]&=3A_1+2A_2,\\ h[4]&=3A_2. \end{aligned}\]Since the filter is fourth order,\[M=5.\]Using symmetry,\[h[0]=h[4] \quad\Rightarrow\quad A_0=3A_2,\]and\[h[1]=h[3]\]gives\[2A_0+A_1 = 3A_1+2A_2.\]Substituting\[A_0=3A_2,\]\[6A_2+A_1 = 3A_1+2A_2,\]\[2A_2=A_1.\]Choosing\[A_2=1,\]gives\[A_1=2, \qquad A_0=3.\]Therefore,\[G(z)=3+2z^{-1}+z^{-2}.\]\[\boxed{\text{(A) }3+2z^{-1}+z^{-2}}\]
Key points
  • A linear-phase FIR filter has a symmetric impulse response.
  • Expand the polynomial first to obtain the impulse-response coefficients.
  • Use symmetry equations to determine the unknown coefficients.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not equate polynomial coefficients directly without expansion.
  • Remember that a fourth-order FIR filter has \(5\) coefficients.
  • Apply the symmetry relation correctly: \(h[n]=h[M-1-n]\).

questions.question: The given figure shows a 3-bit ripple counter, with \(Q_2\) as MSB. The flip-flops are rising edge triggered. The counting direction is:
options: up or down depending on the initial state of \(Q_0\) only
up or down depending on the initial states of \(Q_0,\) \(Q_1,\) \(Q_2\)
questions.explanation:
From figure, (i) It is a positive edge-triggered flip-flop. (ii) Normal output of one flip-flop is used as clock input for next flip-flop. (iii) Output of counter is taken from normal output of final flip-flop. It is an 8-bit down counter. \[\boxed{(A) \; \text{always down}}\]
Key points
  • In ripple counters, "normal output drives next clock" + "positive edge-triggered" combination is the standard signature of a down-counter; if instead the complemented output drove the next clock, it would be an up-counter.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: An 8-bit ADC, with 2's complement output has a nominal input range of -2 V to +2 V . It generates a digital code of 00 H for an analog input in the range -7.8125 mV to +7.815 mV. An input of -1.5 V will produce a digital output of
questions.explanation:
Given:
  • Nominal input (\(V_{i}\)) range is -2 V to +2 V , i.e. , \(V_{max}\) = 2 V and \(V_{min}\) = -2 V
  • Number of bits \(n\) = 8
  • It generates a digital code of 00 H for an analog input in the range -7.8125 mV to +7.815 mV, which implies that 0 V is coded as 00 H.
Resolution/step size is given by: \[\text{Step size } = \frac{V_{max} - V_{min}}{2^n-1} = \frac{4}{2^8-1} = 15.6 \text{ mV}\] To reach -1.5 V , no. of steps required is: \[\text{ Number of steps required } = \frac{1.5}{15.6 \times 10^{-3}} = 95.62 \approx 96\] Therefore the digital output is -(96)\(_{10}\). \[\text{2's complement of -(96)}_{10} = 1010 \;\; 0000 = \text{A0 H}\] \[\boxed{(D) \; \text{A0 H} }\]

questions.ref: Block Diagram and Signal Flow Graph Q1
questions.question: A filter is represented by the signal flow graph shown in the figure. Its input is \(x(t)\) and output is \(y(t)\). The transfer function of the filter is
questions.explanation:
Using Mason's Gain Formula, we analyze the signal flow graph:
  • Forward paths: \(P_1 = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{s}\right) \cdot 1 = -\dfrac{1}{s}\), \(P_2 = 1 \cdot k \cdot 1 \cdot (-1) = -k\)
  • Individual loop: \(L_1 = 1 \cdot k \cdot 1 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{s}\right) = -\dfrac{k}{s}\)
  • Path factors: Since the individual loop touches both forward paths, \(\Delta_1 = 1\) and \(\Delta_2 = 1\).
The system determinant is \(\Delta = 1 - L_1 = 1 - \left(-\dfrac{k}{s}\right) = 1 + \dfrac{k}{s}\). The overall transfer function is: \[T(s) = \frac{P_1\Delta_1 + P_2\Delta_2}{\Delta} = \frac{-\dfrac{1}{s} + (-k)}{1 + \dfrac{k}{s}} = \frac{\dfrac{-(1 + sk)}{s}}{\dfrac{s + k}{s}} = \frac{-(1 + sk)}{s + k}\] \[\boxed{(A) \ \ \dfrac{-(1+ks)}{s+k}}\]

questions.question:
Data for Q3.11.2. The open-loop transfer function of a unity negative feedback control system is given by \[G(s)=\frac{K}{(s+5)^3}\] The 1st Question is given in Unit VI (Q6.11.1)

A unity feedback system has the transfer function \(\dfrac{K(s + b)}{s^2(s + 20)}\) The value of \(b\) for which the loci of all the three roots of the closed loop characteristic equation meet at a single point is
questions.explanation: The characteristic equation for the given unity feedback system (\(H(s) = 1\)) is: \(1 + G(s)H(s) = 0\) \[1 + \frac{K(s + b)}{s^2(s + 20)} = 0 \implies K = -\frac{s^3 + 20s^2}{s + b}\] To find the breakaway or break-in points where the roots meet, we set \(\dfrac{dK}{ds} = 0\): \[\frac{(s + b)(3s^2 + 40s) - (s^3 + 20s^2)(1)}{(s + b)^2} = 0\] \[s\left[2s^2 + (3b + 20)s + 40b\right] = 0\] Thus, \(s = 0\) is one intersection point. For all three roots to meet at a single point, the remaining two roots from the quadratic equation must also coincide at \(s = 0\). For a single point of convergence, the discriminant of the quadratic factor \(2s^2 + (3b + 20)s + 40b = 0\) must be zero (\(B^2 - 4AC = 0\)): \[(3b + 20)^2 - 4(2)(40b) = 0\] \[9b^2 - 200b + 400 = 0\] \[(b - 20)\left(b - \frac{20}{9}\right) = 0 \implies b = 20 \text{ or } b = \frac{20}{9}\] If \(b = 20\), the open-loop zero at \(s = -20\) cancels the open-loop pole at \(s = -20\), reducing the system to a second-order system (only 2 roots total), which contradicts having three roots. \[\boxed{(B) \ \ \dfrac{20}{9}}\]

A linear time-invariant causal system has a frequency response given in polar form as \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+\omega^2}}\angle-\tan^{-1}\omega.\) For input \(x(t)=\sin t\), the output is
questions.explanation:
The input is \(x(t)=\sin t.\) Hence, the excitation frequency is \(\omega=1\,\text{rad/s}.\) The frequency response at \(\omega=1\) is \[H(j1)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+1^2}}\angle-\tan^{-1}(1)
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\angle-\frac{\pi}{4}\] For an LTI system, the output sinusoid has the same frequency, while its amplitude is multiplied by \(|H(j\omega)|\) and its phase is shifted by \(\angle H(j\omega)\). Therefore, \[y(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sin\left(t-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\] \[\boxed{(D)\;\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sin\!\left(t-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)}\]

The open-loop transfer function is, \[T(s)=\frac{K}{s(s+a)}\] Given, \(PM=60^\circ\) and \(\omega_{gc}=1\,\text{rad/s}\) As, \[PM=180^\circ+\angle T(j\omega)\Big|_{\omega=1}\] \[60^\circ

\right)_{\omega=1}\] \[\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{a}=30^\circ\] \[\therefore\quad
a=\sqrt3\] The inserted element is, \(G_c(s)=\dfrac{s-\sqrt3}{s+\sqrt3}\) At \(\omega=1\,\text{rad/s}\), \(|G_c(j1)|=1\). Hence, the gain crossover frequency remains unchanged at \(\omega_{gc}=1\,\text{rad/s}\) When two transfer functions are connected in cascade, \[|GH|=|G||H|,
\qquad
\angle(GH)=\angle G+\angle H\] The phase of the inserted element at \(\omega=1\) is, \(\angle G_c(j1)
=
-2\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}
=-60^\circ\) The original phase at the gain crossover frequency is, \(\angle T(j1)

-180^\circ+60^\circ
=
-120^\circ\) Therefore, the new phase at the gain crossover frequency is \(\angle T'(j1)
=
-120^\circ-60^\circ
=
-180^\circ\) Hence, \[PM
=
180^\circ+\angle T'(j1)
=
180^\circ-180^\circ
=
0^\circ\] \[\boxed{(A)\;0^\circ}\]
